screens.title: Enemy Scene Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A reusable enemy scene typically starts with CharacterBody2D as the root. CharacterBody2D gives you direct, script-driven movement and the ability to call move_and_slide with velocity vectors, which makes patrolling and controlled motion straightforward. Attach a Sprite2D for visuals so the enemy has a drawable representation, and add a CollisionShape2D to match the sprite so physical collisions behave predictably with floors and walls. Add an Area2D child for damage detection; this Area2D is separate from the physical collision so it can be tuned for attack range without affecting movement collision. A dedicated DamageArea prevents confusing physical collisions with attack logic, and it lets you connect body_entered and area_entered signals to call damage handlers. For example, a red enemy might have a slightly larger DamageArea so touching its weapon or body counts as a hit while standing next to it does not. A common misconception is treating the main collision shape as the attack hitbox: that approach mixes responsibilities and makes it hard to time attacks or implement temporary invincibility. The clean separation of movement, visual, and hit detection leads to flexible code and easier debugging. Takeaway: structure scenes by responsibility so AI, collision, and combat code remain clear and testable.

screens.title: Create Enemy.tscn — Step by Step
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a clear step sequence to create a reusable Enemy. tscn. First, create a new 2D scene and set the root to CharacterBody2D, then rename the node to Enemy. This choice gives you access to move_and_slide behavior and consistent collision handling. Second, add a Sprite2D child and assign a simple icon or sprite so you can see the enemy in the editor. Third, add a CollisionShape2D and choose a shape (rectangle or capsule) that matches the sprite; this keeps physical interactions correct. Fourth, add an Area2D child and name it DamageArea, then give it its own CollisionShape2D slightly larger or shaped for attack reach. Fifth, attach an Enemy. gd script to the root and export variables like speed, health, patrol_distance, and damage_to_player so you can tune behavior in the inspector. Finally, connect DamageArea's body_entered signal to a handler that checks for the Player node and applies damage. A concrete example: set speed to fifty, health to three, and a patrol_distance of one hundred. Misconception: do not forget to set the CollisionShape2D disabled state for unused shapes; an unintended enabled shape can block movement. Takeaway: building the scene deliberately makes scripting and testing straightforward.

screens.title: Patrolling AI Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Patrolling is a beginner-friendly AI that produces predictable enemy movement. The pattern uses a current_direction variable with values 1 for right and -1 for left, a start_x to record the spawn position, and a patrol_distance to define how far the enemy travels before reversing direction. In each physics frame set velocity. x to speed times current_direction, then check whether global_position. x has passed the start_x plus or minus the patrol_distance. If so, invert current_direction so the enemy heads back the other way. Apply gravity if your enemy can fall, and then call move_and_slide to perform movement with built-in collision resolution. A concrete example: if start_x is 200 and patrol_distance is 100, the enemy moves between x=100 and x=300. A common misconception is using position changes without move_and_slide; doing so bypasses collision resolution and can allow the enemy to clip through floors. Another pitfall is not storing start_x in _ready, which leads to patrol boundaries recalculating incorrectly after instancing. Takeaway: this simple pattern gives reliable, tunable enemy motion that is easy to extend for chasing behavior later. Patrolling AI Logic means use start_x, patrol_distance, and current_direction with move_and_slide to create back-and-forth movement.. In practical terms, implementing a simple back-and-forth enemy movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 03 › Chapter 3.3 › Patrolling AI
Core loop
Maintain current_direction, set velocity.x = speed * current_direction, check global_position.x against start_x ± patrol_distance, invert direction when limit reached, apply gravity if airborne, and call move_and_slide.
Example values
speed = 50, patrol_distance = 100, start_x recorded on _ready. Enemy travels between start_x - 100 and start_x + 100.
Misconception
Avoid setting global_position directly each frame. Use move_and_slide so collisions are resolved and the enemy doesn't clip through environment geometry.
Visualization
Range
Start position anchors the patrol center. Boundaries become start_x ± patrol_distance so you can tune how wide the enemy roams.
Key Takeaway

Patrols are deterministic and easy to tune; store anchor positions and always use physics-aware movement calls.

screens.title: CharacterBody2D vs RigidBody2D
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right root node depends on how you want the enemy to behave. CharacterBody2D is ideal when you need direct, script-driven motion such as patrols, chasing, or precise platformer-style movement. It lets you set velocity and call move_and_slide, so you maintain control over movement and collision response. RigidBody2D, by contrast, is better for physics-driven objects like rolling boulders or debris where forces, impulses, and realistic physics response are desirable. A common beginner mistake is forcing AI-like movement inside a RigidBody2D by repeatedly setting its position; this fights the physics engine and produces unstable results. Another misconception is assuming CharacterBody2D can't react to physics—CharacterBody2D can still detect collisions and respond to gravity if you implement it. Concrete scenario: for a patrolling guard that turns around at boundaries, CharacterBody2D is the correct choice because you want deterministic back-and-forth motion and to call move_and_slide to keep collisions stable. Takeaway: prefer CharacterBody2D for controlled AI movement, and use RigidBody2D for objects whose primary behavior should be dictated by physics. screens.title: Area2D for Combat Collision
screens.narratorSegment: Area2D is the recommended mechanism for detecting combat interactions because it signals overlaps rather than enforcing physical responses. Use an Area2D as a DamageArea to trigger damage when a player enters it, or use an attack Area2D on the player that emits area_entered when a swing or projectile overlaps an enemy. This separation makes it clear which interactions should deal damage and when. A concrete example: add a DamageArea child to the enemy that connects its body_entered signal to an enemy function that checks if the entering body is the Player, then calls the player's _take_damage method. One common misunderstanding is trying to use collision response from CharacterBody2D as an attack trigger; that often results in unwanted hits while the player is merely colliding with the enemy's physics body. Another pitfall is not using name checks or groups; always confirm the entering body is the intended target before applying damage. Takeaway: Area2D provides precise, frame-independent overlap events that make combat logic explicit and controllable. How to use
Add an Area2D as a child and attach a CollisionShape2D. For enemy damage to player, connect DamageArea.body_entered to a handler that checks the colliding body. For player attacks, activate an Area2D during the attack animation and listen for area_entered on enemies.

screens.title: Enemy.gd — Patrolling and Health
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concise enemy script that implements patrolling and a health system. The script exports speed, health, and patrol_distance so you can tune enemy behavior without changing code. In _ready the script records start_x to anchor the patrol and connects the DamageArea. body_entered signal. In _physics_process the script sets velocity. x based on current_direction and flips direction when the enemy crosses its patrol bounds, then uses move_and_slide to perform movement with gravity applied if not on the floor. The _take_damage function subtracts from health, prints a debug message, and calls queue_free when health falls to zero or below. A concrete example of misuse is subtracting health but forgetting to call queue_free; that leaves a dead enemy object visible and possibly blocking gameplay. Another mistake is calling free instead of queue_free while the node is still being processed — queue_free schedules safe removal. This pattern centralizes damage handling and keeps the runtime tidy. # Enemy.gd
extends CharacterBody2D

@export var speed: float = 50.0

@export var patrol_distance: float = 100.0
@export var damage_to_player: int = 1

var current_direction: int = 1
var start_x: float

func _ready() -> void:
  start_x = global_position.x
  $DamageArea.body_entered.connect(_on_DamageArea_body_entered)

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
  velocity.x = speed * current_direction

  if current_direction == 1 and global_position.x >= start_x + patrol_distance:
    current_direction = -1
  elif current_direction == -1 and global_position.x <= start_x - patrol_distance:
    current_direction = 1

  if not is_on_floor():
    velocity.y += 400 * delta

  move_and_slide()

func _take_damage(amount: int) -> void:
  health -= amount
  print("Enemy took ", amount, " damage. Health: ", health)
  if health <= 0:
    print("Enemy defeated!")
    queue_free()
Explanation
The exported variables are inspector-tunable. start_x anchors the patrol. move_and_slide resolves collisions and gravity. _take_damage centralizes health checks and removal via queue_free.
Key Takeaway

This script is a template: tune exported values for each enemy variant and keep damage handling centralized for clarity.

screens.title: Common Combat Mistakes & Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Combat systems are full of small pitfalls that become obvious during playtesting. One common mistake is confusing CharacterBody2D collision responses with Area2D overlap events. This often leads to accidental damage when the player merely touches an enemy's physics body. Fix this by relocating attack triggers to an Area2D and checking signals explicitly. Another mistake is using free instead of queue_free, which can raise errors if the node is still being processed; queue_free is the safe choice because it defers removal. Missing or incorrect name checks are frequent sources of runtime errors — prefer method existence checks and groups over brittle node names. Continuous damage every frame is usually due to applying damage inside _physics_process while the player remains in a DamageArea; instead, use body_entered to trigger damage or implement a damage timer that ticks at controlled intervals, and stop it on body_exited. Finally, forgetting to store start_x causes patrols to drift when instanced; record anchor positions in _ready. Takeaway: test interactions deliberately, read the console for signal or method errors, and keep responsibilities separate so each system is easier to verify.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to add meaningful challenge to your game by building basic enemy characters and simple combat systems. We'll use CharacterBody2D as the enemy root for scripted movement and collision handling, add an Area2D hitbox for damage interactions, and implement a health system with a _take_damage function that calls queue_free when an enemy is defeated. You will see a concrete patrolling example, learn how to connect Area2D signals for reliable hit detection, and understand how to safely reload the scene when the player dies. These are practical, repeatable patterns: enemy scene setup, patrolling logic, damage detection, and defeat handling. Knowing when to use CharacterBody2D versus physics-driven bodies prevents common bugs when hitboxes and collisions interact. By the end you should be comfortable instancing enemies into your main scene, verifying that collisions only damage intended targets, and cleaning up defeated nodes without runtime errors. Think about one enemy behavior you want in your game — after this lesson you’ll be able to implement it and control its lifecycle with confidence.

These learning objectives lay out practical skills you will gain. First, you will design and implement enemy characters using CharacterBody2D so they move and collide like your player. This matters because scripted movement and consistent collision behavior make interactions reliable. Second, you will develop simple enemy AI such as patrolling or following a path, learning how a direction variable and patrol distance produce repeatable movement. Third, you will implement collision detection for combat using Area2D so hits are precise and controllable, avoiding accidental damage from physical collisions. Fourth, you will create a basic health system for both player and enemy with a _take_damage function that centralizes damage logic. Each objective connects to a verified competency milestone — by the end you should be able to build an Enemy. tscn, wire signals, and demonstrate enemies that deal and receive damage without causing scene errors. These skills are foundational for reusable enemy behaviors and stable playtesting.

This continuation emphasizes the wiring and integration tasks you will practice. You will connect Area2D signals for damage so events trigger the correct _take_damage handlers and do not fire for other collisions. This skill matters because signals are the reliable glue between scene parts and prevent accidental damage to the wrong node. You will also learn to integrate your Enemy. tscn instances into your main scene, positioning them and verifying behavior across multiple enemies. Testing includes observing health reductions, confirming enemies call queue_free when defeated, and checking that the player restarts the scene when health reaches zero. Finally, you will practice safe removal patterns — specifically queue_free instead of free — to avoid runtime errors if a node is still being processed. These skills make your game resilient during development and testing, improving iteration speed and player experience.

A reusable enemy scene typically starts with CharacterBody2D as the root. CharacterBody2D gives you direct, script-driven movement and the ability to call move_and_slide with velocity vectors, which makes patrolling and controlled motion straightforward. Attach a Sprite2D for visuals so the enemy has a drawable representation, and add a CollisionShape2D to match the sprite so physical collisions behave predictably with floors and walls. Add an Area2D child for damage detection; this Area2D is separate from the physical collision so it can be tuned for attack range without affecting movement collision. A dedicated DamageArea prevents confusing physical collisions with attack logic, and it lets you connect body_entered and area_entered signals to call damage handlers. For example, a red enemy might have a slightly larger DamageArea so touching its weapon or body counts as a hit while standing next to it does not. A common misconception is treating the main collision shape as the attack hitbox: that approach mixes responsibilities and makes it hard to time attacks or implement temporary invincibility. The clean separation of movement, visual, and hit detection leads to flexible code and easier debugging. Takeaway: structure scenes by responsibility so AI, collision, and combat code remain clear and testable.

Follow a clear step sequence to create a reusable Enemy. tscn. First, create a new 2D scene and set the root to CharacterBody2D, then rename the node to Enemy. This choice gives you access to move_and_slide behavior and consistent collision handling. Second, add a Sprite2D child and assign a simple icon or sprite so you can see the enemy in the editor. Third, add a CollisionShape2D and choose a shape (rectangle or capsule) that matches the sprite; this keeps physical interactions correct. Fourth, add an Area2D child and name it DamageArea, then give it its own CollisionShape2D slightly larger or shaped for attack reach. Fifth, attach an Enemy. gd script to the root and export variables like speed, health, patrol_distance, and damage_to_player so you can tune behavior in the inspector. Finally, connect DamageArea's body_entered signal to a handler that checks for the Player node and applies damage. A concrete example: set speed to fifty, health to three, and a patrol_distance of one hundred. Misconception: do not forget to set the CollisionShape2D disabled state for unused shapes; an unintended enabled shape can block movement. Takeaway: building the scene deliberately makes scripting and testing straightforward.

Patrolling is a beginner-friendly AI that produces predictable enemy movement. The pattern uses a current_direction variable with values 1 for right and -1 for left, a start_x to record the spawn position, and a patrol_distance to define how far the enemy travels before reversing direction. In each physics frame set velocity. x to speed times current_direction, then check whether global_position. x has passed the start_x plus or minus the patrol_distance. If so, invert current_direction so the enemy heads back the other way. Apply gravity if your enemy can fall, and then call move_and_slide to perform movement with built-in collision resolution. A concrete example: if start_x is 200 and patrol_distance is 100, the enemy moves between x=100 and x=300. A common misconception is using position changes without move_and_slide; doing so bypasses collision resolution and can allow the enemy to clip through floors. Another pitfall is not storing start_x in _ready, which leads to patrol boundaries recalculating incorrectly after instancing. Takeaway: this simple pattern gives reliable, tunable enemy motion that is easy to extend for chasing behavior later. Patrolling AI Logic means use start_x, patrol_distance, and current_direction with move_and_slide to create back-and-forth movement.. In practical terms, implementing a simple back-and-forth enemy movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the right root node depends on how you want the enemy to behave. CharacterBody2D is ideal when you need direct, script-driven motion such as patrols, chasing, or precise platformer-style movement. It lets you set velocity and call move_and_slide, so you maintain control over movement and collision response. RigidBody2D, by contrast, is better for physics-driven objects like rolling boulders or debris where forces, impulses, and realistic physics response are desirable. A common beginner mistake is forcing AI-like movement inside a RigidBody2D by repeatedly setting its position; this fights the physics engine and produces unstable results. Another misconception is assuming CharacterBody2D can't react to physics—CharacterBody2D can still detect collisions and respond to gravity if you implement it. Concrete scenario: for a patrolling guard that turns around at boundaries, CharacterBody2D is the correct choice because you want deterministic back-and-forth motion and to call move_and_slide to keep collisions stable. Takeaway: prefer CharacterBody2D for controlled AI movement, and use RigidBody2D for objects whose primary behavior should be dictated by physics. CharacterBody2D vs RigidBody2D means characterbody2d for scripted ai movement; rigidbody2d for physics-first objects like rolling hazards.. In practical terms, which to use for different enemy behaviors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Area2D is the recommended mechanism for detecting combat interactions because it signals overlaps rather than enforcing physical responses. Use an Area2D as a DamageArea to trigger damage when a player enters it, or use an attack Area2D on the player that emits area_entered when a swing or projectile overlaps an enemy. This separation makes it clear which interactions should deal damage and when. A concrete example: add a DamageArea child to the enemy that connects its body_entered signal to an enemy function that checks if the entering body is the Player, then calls the player's _take_damage method. One common misunderstanding is trying to use collision response from CharacterBody2D as an attack trigger; that often results in unwanted hits while the player is merely colliding with the enemy's physics body. Another pitfall is not using name checks or groups; always confirm the entering body is the intended target before applying damage. Takeaway: Area2D provides precise, frame-independent overlap events that make combat logic explicit and controllable. Area2D for Combat Collision means area2d detects overlaps for combat without affecting physics, enabling clear attack-hit separation and reliable signals.. In practical terms, why area2d is the correct tool for hit detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a concise enemy script that implements patrolling and a health system. The script exports speed, health, and patrol_distance so you can tune enemy behavior without changing code. In _ready the script records start_x to anchor the patrol and connects the DamageArea. body_entered signal. In _physics_process the script sets velocity. x based on current_direction and flips direction when the enemy crosses its patrol bounds, then uses move_and_slide to perform movement with gravity applied if not on the floor.
